To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
iNOS(-/) mice are unable to clear sub-clinical bacterial infection due to a defect in AM function, while gp91(phox(-/-) mice are not compromised in their ability to control bacterial growth.
iNOS(-/-) mice have reduced AM apoptosis and increased neutrophilic inflammation during subclinical pneumococcal infection, while ROS deficiency has no effect on innate host defense.
iNOS is essential for the generation of apoptotic macrophages in the lung during sub-clinical pneumococcal infection, while ROS are not essential for this function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of ROS and NO in AM apoptosis and the innate response to sub-clinical bacterial challenge.
the innate response to low-level bacterial infection and the mechanisms by which AM function is impaired in the absence of iNOS or gp91phox.
the innate immune response to bacterial infection in the lungs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
iNOS is required for AM function and apoptosis in the innate response of the lung to low dose bacterial challenge.
NO is required for AM apoptosis in this model but that NO and ROS are both required for optimal innate immunity to pneumococcal infection.
iNOS is required for AM apoptosis and that ROS is required for AM function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ROS and NO have contrasting roles in the pulmonary response to S. pneumoniae infection, with NO playing a critical role in AM apoptosis and ROS playing an inhibitory role in AM competence.
NO is required for AM apoptosis and subsequent resolution of infection.
iNOS is essential for AM apoptosis, while ROS are dispensable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NO and ROS play contrasting roles in the AM response to low-dosage bacterial infection.
the production of NO is critical to the innate immune response to subclinical S. pneumoniae infection.
ROS production by phagocytes plays an important role in the innate response and is essential for the induction of apoptosis of AM infected with low-dose Streptococcus.
